items.headline: Zelensky urges US and Musk to lift Starlink restrictions and be on 'right side of history'
items.blurb: The Ukrainian president says the slowed-down internet is making it difficult to stop Russian attacks.
items.text: A crucial US satellite internet service is still operating too slowly and affecting Ukraine's ability to stop Russian attacks, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said. "We are counting on these restrictions being lifted. The protection of lives and Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of winter directly depends on this," he said. The issue over the speed of the Starshield system - a military-grade Starlink service owned by Elon Musk and provided to Ukraine by the US government - has been rumbling on for weeks. Zelensky said he had asked officials "to work as closely as possible" with the US government and Musk's company. "It is important to be on the right side of history," he said. The BBC has asked the White House and Starlink for comment. Ukraine uses the normal Starlink service for communications on the battlefield, while Starshield is used for the interception of missiles and drones in Ukraine airspace. items.headline: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza cleared of using AI to write prize-winning story
items.blurb: After a month-long investigation it was concluded that Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which won the £10,000 Caine prize, was ‘human-written’ The Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded…
items.text: After a month-long investigation it was concluded that Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which won the £10,000 Caine prize, was ‘human-written’ The Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded that his entry was “human-written” after a month-long investigation. Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter , which charts the declining fortunes of a family after the father invests in fish tanks, was announced as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October. Five days later, the Atlantic published an article titled “Yet another literary prize winner seems to be AI”, in which the author and journalist Vauhini Vara said the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated. The Caine prize chair, Ellah Wakatama, said in a statement : “From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human-written. items.headline: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
items.blurb: The Nvidia scandal has raised questions over whether advanced AI chips ended up in China, despite US restrictions.
items.text: Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the company says. Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees. Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions. The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business. Megaspeed said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence". It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". items.blurb: Seven-time F1 world champion tours border area and logistics warehouses operated by Egyptian Red Crescent Lewis Hamilton has visited Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with the Gaza Strip to meet organisations sending humanitarian aid to the territory.
items.text: Seven-time F1 world champion tours border area and logistics warehouses operated by Egyptian Red Crescent Lewis Hamilton has visited Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with the Gaza Strip to meet organisations sending humanitarian aid to the territory. The seven-time Formula One world champion has spoken out about conflict and humanitarian crises in the region, and has called for peace. He has frequently posted on social media about children killed in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza and called for a ceasefire. “I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine . I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping we get to at some stage,” Hamilton said in October. A ceasefire agreement reached last year has halted major combat operations in Gaza, but the amount of aid reaching the territory continues to fall far short of the agreed-upon minimum of 600 trucks a day. items.headline: Australian MP who lost both legs in alleged car attack discharged from hospital
items.blurb: The MP was allegedly run down by a car outside her electorate office four weeks ago.
items.text: Australian politician Helen Haines, who lost both of her legs after police say she was deliberately run down with a car, has been discharged from hospital. The independent MP was struck outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, north-east of Melbourne, on October 19, in an alleged attack which horrified Australia. Brendan Nugent, 43, has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the federal offence of causing harm to a public official. He is yet to enter pleas. Haines, 65, has been discharged, the Alfred Hospital said on Monday, after four weeks and several surgeries which resulted in the amputation of her legs. Haines, known for supporting stronger climate action and helping establish a national anti-corruption commission, entered parliament in 2019 as the Member for Indi after working as a nurse and midwife. Victoria Police has said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police, remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established. items.blurb: Pope Leo XIV warns deforestation and illegal mining are threatening the Amazon rainforest and the local communities.
items.text: Pope Leo XIV warned that deforestation and illegal mining are threatening the Amazon rainforest and the communities living there. He said protecting the environment, ensuring social justice and safeguarding local communities must go hand in hand.

items.headline: Collision of two trains in Egypt kills at least seven
items.blurb: President orders prompt investigation after one train derails in collision in al-Ayyat about 50km from Cairo Seven people were killed and at least 125 injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, officials said.
items.text: President orders prompt investigation after one train derails in collision in al-Ayyat about 50km from Cairo Seven people were killed and at least 125 injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, officials said. The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 50km (30 miles) south of Cairo, when a train travelling to Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the transport ministry. An inspection indicated that the Cairo-Aswan train had been stationary on the same track, officials said. The health ministry gave the casualty toll, adding more than 70 of the injured were discharged after receiving treatment. Train derailments and crashes are common in Egypt, where the railway system has a history of mismanagement and poor maintenance of equipment. In recent years the government has announced modernisation initiatives to improve its railways. items.headline: Mexican drug lord Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo dies age 80
items.blurb: Known as the 'Boss of Bosses', he was the head of all-powerful Guadalajara Cartel in the 1980s before his arrest broke up his drug organisation.
items.text: Notorious Mexican drug lord Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo has died in hospital aged 80. Félix Gallardo was widely considered one of the biggest drug smugglers in history and is credited with building an alliance between criminal groups in Colombia and his own Mexican cartel. Known as The Godfather or the 'Boss of Bosses', Félix Gallardo was the head of the all-powerful Guadalajara Cartel, which reigned over Mexican drug trafficking at the height of the cocaine boom of the 1980s. At the time, it created a new modus operandi in the illegal drug trade which endures to this day. He had been in state custody since 1989. The name Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo will echo through the annals of drug-trafficking history more than any other except perhaps Pablo Escobar's. He led the organisation which revolutionised drug smuggling in the region by entering into partnership with the Colombian cartels, particularly Escobar's Medellín Cartel, to combine production in the Andes with Mexican transportation across the border into the United States. items.headline: Increase in government health spending as out-of-pocket expenditure declines: Report
items.text: Even as the country’s economy has grown, people have been spending a smaller and smaller share of it on healthcare while government spending has remained below 2% of GDP, according to the recently released National Health Accounts Estimates for 2023–24. The National Health Policy 2017 had set a target of raising government health spending to 2.5% of GDP by 2025. The data show that total expenditure on healthcare — that includes government spending, insurance payments and out-of-pocket payments — remained at 3.3% of GDP in 2023–24. This was lower than the 3.8% recorded during the pandemic year of 2021–22 (there was a change in the GDP base year for the calculations over the last two years for which the estimates are available). Healthcare spending as a proportion of GDP has remained low even as the absolute amount spent per capita has gone up — meaning that healthcare spending has not kept pace with the growing economy. items.headline: Buddha relics arrive at Arunachal’s Golden Pagoda for final phase of exposition
items.blurb: The Namsai exposition follows a six-day programme at Bomdila’s Thubchog Gatsel Ling Monastery from November 8 to 13, which attracted more than 35,000 devotees
items.text: The sacred relics of Shakyamuni Buddha arrived at the Golden Pagoda in Namsai, Arunachal Pradesh, on Friday, marking the final phase of their exposition in the state, which has already drawn more than 66,000 devotees at Tawang and Bomdila. The relics were received at Nalung Helipad by Arunachal Pradesh governor Lt Gen Kaiwalya Trivikram Parnaik (retd), accompanied by deputy chief minister Chowna Mein, state ministers, public representatives and Buddhist religious leaders. They were subsequently taken in a ceremonial procession and enshrined at the Golden Pagoda, also known as Kongmu Kham. The governor inaugurated the exposition, which will remain open for public darshan from November 14 to 20. Addressing the gathering, he said the relics symbolised Buddha’s life, enlightenment and timeless teachings, adding that the principles of peace, compassion, wisdom and non-violence were particularly relevant amid growing conflict and intolerance across the world. Parnaik highlighted Arunachal Pradesh’s diverse Buddhist traditions, including Mahayana, Vajrayana and Theravada, and described the exposition as a rare opportunity for devotees to reconnect with Buddha’s teachings. items.headline: Taming of ‘Kabra Kaan’: Meet the 3,000-kg tusker that has 100 forest officials on their toes
items.text: 100 forest officials, three veterinary doctors, two trained elephants, numerous volunteers, and drones: For the last four days, all of these have been deployed in the jungles of Chhattisgarh to track a 3,000-kg elephant. Known to have gone Musth (aggressive), the 20-year-old elephant has allegedly killed 16 people in the state’s northern region in the last few months. Last week, the department finally received the permission to tranquilise the tusker. There is one problem, though: Likely aware that it is being trailed, the elephant has joined a herd of other tuskers to avoid being identified, said an official. Over the last six to seven months, Kabra Kaan, named so due to the pigmentation in its ear, has allegedly trampled to death at least 16 people and injured a few more. It has been moving in a radius of 75 kms in the dense jungle areas of four districts: Korea, Surguja, Surajpur and Balrampur. items.headline: Rajasthan railway blast accused have ISI links: Police
items.blurb: Investigators allege they made two earlier attempts to blow up the line. The blast damaged railway sleepers but caused no injuries.
items.text: Two people arrested from Punjab in connection with the November 3 railway track blast in Sri Ganganagar district of Rajasthan are suspected to have links with Pakistan ’s Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI) and had made two unsuccessful attempts to blow up the railway line before carrying out the explosion earlier this month, police said on Sunday. The November 3 blast occurred near 50 GB village on the Anupgarh-Suratgarh railway line, close to the India - Pakistan border. Although there were no injuries, the blast damaged two concrete sleepers and left a crater around two feet deep. The accused, identified as Mehakdeep Kaur (21) and Devendra Singh (23), were arrested on Saturday from Gurdaspur in Punjab. Police said they recovered two foreign-made pistols, 46 live cartridges and ₹ 30,000 allegedly received for carrying out the blast.

They are found on every continent except Antarctica and count over 29,500 native species worldwide. According to Orchids of India: A Pictorial Guide (2019), published by the Botanical Survey of India, Keralam accounts for more than a third of the 307 endemic orchids reported from India. The State’s native orchid density is comparable to South American countries like Costa Rica, Viswambharan Sarasan, a research leader at the Royal Botanic Gardens in the U.K., said. items.headline: CBI arrests two NCB staffers for demanding Rs 25 lakh bribe from a chemist in UP
items.text: Two sub-inspectors posted with the Narcotics Control Bureau have been arrested by the CBI for allegedly demanding Rs 25 lakh from a Uttar Pradesh-based chemist to keep him out of a narcotics case. On Saturday, the arrest unfolded in a high-voltage chase at Tamil Sangam Marg in R K Puram, where CBI personnel pursued both officers. In an application filed before the Special Judge, CBI, at Rouse Avenue courts, the CBI Sunday sought two days’ police custody of the arrested SIs — Ajit Singh Meena and Sumeet Kumar — to recover the alleged bribe money, trace mobile phones and SIM cards, and investigate the involvement of “other officials”. The CBI registered the case on November 14 after a complaint from Amin Shukla, proprietor of Sanjeevani Medical Store in Powayan town, Shahjahanpur district. “In his complaint, Shukla alleged that Meena, who was the investigating officer of an NDPS case registered by the NCB’s Delhi Zonal Unit, demanded money for not implicating him in that case. During verification conducted by the CBI on the same day, the demand was prima facie corroborated.

items.headline: Michigan pension fund drags Intel to court after 29% stock plunge in a day wiped out $140 billion in market value
items.blurb: Intel shareholders have filed a proposed class action, alleging the company concealed how slowing PC sales and excess inventory would hurt revenue. The suit says Intel disclosed the problems too late, before its stock plunged 28.6% in one day, wiping out about $140 billion in market value.
items.text: A group of shareholders have sued chipmaker Intel for allegedly defrauding them by concealing the impact of a prolonged slowdown in personal computer sales that caused its stock price to plunge nearly 29% in a single day. According to Reuters, in the proposed class action filed on Friday in the San Jose, California, federal court, shareholders led by a Michigan pension fund said Intel was too slow to disclose information about how slowing PC sales and an inventory glut would weigh on revenue. They argued that Intel's problems with PC sales and excess inventory outweighed data center construction and other benefits related to the artificial intelligence boom. They also said Intel had the motive and opportunity to defraud by raising capital in mid-August, halfway through its "disastrous" third quarter, when it sold $23 billion of stock at $95 per share. The sale came as Intel looked to build out its chip contract manufacturing business, a key part of Chief Executive Lip-Bu Tan 's business strategy. items.text: On November 12, Jensen Huang was forced to step down as CEO of Nvidia, the company he co-founded and led since its inception in 1993, in one of the most polarizing moves in recent corporate history. But just days after his ouster, Huang is already plotting his comeback to the helm of the world’s second-most valuable company. According to The Financial Times , Huang is discussing a return to Nvidia as CEO with some of his closest allies. A Huang ally told FT that they were putting together a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for the former Nvidia chief’s return and would try to garner support from the White House. “Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” the ally said, adding that “The efforts had Huang’s support.” According to a Financial Times report, Huang is discussing a possible return with some of his closest allies. The study will be conducted through a new app where participants can ask health questions and rate the responses. Apple announced a new study today with the goal of better understanding how people interact with conversational AI health tools and how useful their responses actually are. The company is conducting the Apple Health AI Usage Study in collaboration with OpenEvidence , a clinical AI platform used by healthcare professionals that generates answers based on medical information from sources like The New England Journal of Medicine . Participants will use a new iOS app to ask medical questions and then rate the responses based on criteria including accuracy, detail, and relevance. The app is now available for download, and enrollment starts today, with Apple looking for up to 200,000 people to contribute. Participants 21 and older must be based in the US, and although the app doesn’t use Apple Intelligence, it does require an iPhone 15 Pro running iOS 26 or later.

items.text: Google is continuing its elemental AI naming scheme with the new Gemini 4 Hydrogen . Google claims that Hydrogen represents a major improvement versus the previous Flash model. It runs in one of four thinking levels (low, medium, high, and the new xhigh), and even in high mode, it’s 2.5 times faster than Flash 3.8. Plus, it reduces “fabricated claims” by more than 5x, according to Google’s analysis. Users will also see gains in code generation, with Hydrogen more than tripling 3.8 Flash’s score in Terminal-Bench. In some cases, Hydrogen even trades blows with Argon. It managed a score of 54 in the popular Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with xhigh mode versus 50 for Argon. Google believes Hydrogen will be a key part of how developers work with agentic coding tools. items.blurb: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially…
items.text: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.” Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China. It is one of three chip-security bills under consideration for inclusion in the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, each of which is drawing renewed attention after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy. When the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed. In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “new, untested, and potentially infeasible.”

items.blurb: "Jensen is Nvidia, right? And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia."
items.text: We didn’t see this coming. Or at least, I didn’t — a week ago, when I wrote about Nvidia’s board opening an investigation into then-CEO Jensen Huang, I assumed his job was safe. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Rebecca Bellan, Tim De Chant, and I discussed how Huang’s ouster went down and what it means for the larger AI economy. While Tim said he saw it coming (albeit not this quickly), Rebecca said, “I didn’t think it was going to happen at all.” “Jensen is Nvidia, right?” she added. “And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia.” Similarly, I marveled at how quickly Huang’s support seemed to crumble, with more scandals seeming to emerge every day. (At the same time, there are many who’d still like to see him return .) And we also took a moment to wonder what will happen to Nvidia’s investments in the larger AI ecosystem. items.text: Outsiders had little reason to notice when Nvidia’s longtime chief security officer and head of product security stepped down in August. Just two and a half months later, CEO Jensen Huang himself left the company over growing questions about his extramarital relationships — starting with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore data center company that U.S. investigators suspect of funneling Nvidia chips to China, then widening to reports about two separate affairs with Nvidia employees. At the time, David Reber, who spent four years as CSO and seven at Nvidia overall, said he was leaving for health reasons. “This wasn’t a pivot I had planned. But I know what needs to come first: family and health,” he wrote on LinkedIn in late August, disclosing that he’d been diagnosed with young-onset Parkinson’s more than two years ago. Reber’s replacement, Saša Zdjelar, previously spent 17 years at ExxonMobil in Houston, leaving as a senior IT manager before spending one year at Salesforce and several years at the cybersecurity company ReversingLabs. Both Democrats and Republicans have voiced support for various measures and bills that would tighten rules and have demanded that Huang and other Nvidia leaders testify before Congress. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has already said that Huang and the Trump administration need to answer to Congress . Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott has also sent letters to both Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick calling on them to publicly testify to the committee. items.text: As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy. I spoke with Wiener on Friday, only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk. The previous day, the AI nonprofit METR had released a report that had been widely interpreted as evidence that Anthropic had achieved recursive self-improvement, a phenomenon in which AI meaningfully contributes to its own advancement and AI progress potentially spins out of control. “It’s very concerning,” Wiener said, citing the report as evidence that we are quickly running out of time to regulate AI. “It was my hope that Congress would take decisive action before the end of this year,” he said. “That does not appear to be happening.” Wiener has been increasingly focused on AI in recent years, and he’s made many of the AI safety movement’s

items.headline: Google faces calls for AI moratoriums in schools after Gemini pilot backlash
items.blurb: Families confront Google after teen’s lawsuit labels Gemini a “suicide coach.”
items.text: CHICAGO—Families joined protests in seven cities nationwide on Wednesday, rallying against what they see as Google’s bid to entrench its AI models in schools, turn kids of all ages into Gemini guinea pigs, and hook them on AI. The backlash follows a Google statement last week, confirming that there will be no way for students to use Google Search without AI. While Google claimed it was giving schools “more choice, not less”—by turning off Search, Gemini, and Gemini Notebook by default—it would not provide an option that allowed Search without AI. For students, the only way to avoid interacting with AI was to remember to add “-ai” to every query, parents worried. In Chicago, many families showed up to protest Google, despite cold, rainy weather. items.text: CSET’s Helen Toner says ‘we’re screwed’ if our AI safety plan rests on any one person being trusted to get this right. Today, I’m talking with Helen Toner, the executive director of the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. This episode is part two of our series on AI in real life. Helen is a well-known figure in the AI safety and policy community, though she is perhaps best known for having served on the board of OpenAI, when she was one of four board members who voted to fire Sam Altman . That incident, now sometimes referred to as “the blip,” ended with Sam coming back as CEO, Helen resigning, and a new board of directors. OpenAI has since restructured entirely . But it’s worth remembering what Helen and the board were supposed to do: OpenAI’s nonprofit board existed specifically to make sure the company didn’t betray its mission to build safe AI by prioritizing profit and growth over safety. items.text: NVIDIA’s influence in India extends far beyond GPU sales, spanning AI infrastructure, software, developer ecosystems, startup incubation and direct equity investments. With Indian data centre operators committing billions of dollars to NVIDIA-powered infrastructure, and enterprises and startups building on its CUDA-led software stack, the company has become deeply embedded in the country's AI ambitions. As Jensen Huang exits, the bigger question is whether India can reduce its dependence on a single technology provider, particularly as geopolitical uncertainties, export restrictions and competing chip architectures reshape access to AI compute. Jensen Huang’s exit from NVIDIA has put the spotlight on the company’s leadership and succession plans. But for India, the more consequential question is what happens to an ecosystem that has increasingly come to depend on the American chipmaker for its AI ambitions. From data centre operators ordering thousands of GPUs to startups building on its software stack, NVIDIA has established relationships across almost every layer of India’s AI industry.
